source: First, Rabe, Ringer, Brun (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with Large Language Models
finding: A fine-tuned LLM writes a whole Isabelle proof in one shot. A second fine-tuned model then repairs failed proofs using the failed attempt plus the prover error message.
numbers: PISA benchmark. Whole-proof generation alone 47.9% (search-based prior 39.0%). Repair adds 1.5% extra theorems even when compute is matched. Context from the theory file: 47.5% with vs 40.7% without. Baldur+Thor together 65.7% vs Thor alone 57.0%. Ensemble of 10 Baldur models 58.0%.
quote: The error message is crucial for this improvement.
limits: Gain from repair is small in absolute terms (1.5 points). Repair model was fine-tuned, not prompted. Isabelle only; authors note other proof assistants give lower rates.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G2 and S5: a revision that sees the real failing output beats one that does not. But the gain is modest, so repair is a supplement to sampling, not a replacement.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur, repair ablation without error message
finding: A control arm gave the repair model the failed proof but no error message. Figure 5 plots theorems proven against inference cost for Generate, Generate+Repair, and Generate+Repair with no error message.
numbers: Figure 5 read from text: the no-error-message curve gives much less gain than the error-message curve; the paper states the error message is crucial. Exact curve values not in the text.
limits: Only a plot, no table; values for the control arm not stated in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-located failing-output rule: revise from the verifier text, not from re-reading the old attempt.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur, learnable proof search with two repair rounds
finding: Proof-of-concept: generate once, repair once, repair the repair. Compare with plain generation at the same cost.
numbers: Cost 2: generate+repair 24.9%. Second repair adds 1.3% for 26.2% at cost 3. Plain generation at cost 3 gives 25.4%, so second repair beats it by 0.8 points (temperature 0).
limits: Repair-of-repair data was not in training; authors say the model only learned first-round repairs. Small margin, single run.
agent_relevance: Repeated repair gives shrinking returns. Cap repair depth in S5 at about 1-2 rounds unless new information (new error) arrives.

source: Lu, Delaware, Zhang (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM), ASE 2024
finding: Generate-then-repair for Coq. First study of 10,000+ LLM proof errors gave a taxonomy; then hand-built symbolic repair rules fix common errors; CoqHammer is a fallback; backtracking regenerates earlier steps when repair fails.
numbers: Benchmark 10,826 theorems from 27 Coq projects. Error taxonomy: wrong theorem application 49.6%, invalid reference 15.2%, incorrect rewrite 11.7%, redundant introductions 10.8%, tactic misuse 8.5%, bullet misuse 3.7%, misc 0.6%. Results: GPT-3.5 alone 402 (3.7%) vs +PALM 4377 (40.4%); GPT-4o 689 (6.4%) vs 4614 (42.6%); Llama-3-70B 386 (3.6%) vs 4155 (38.3%); Llama-3-8B 7 (0.1%) vs 3433 (31.7%). Baselines: Passport 14.4%, Proverbot9001 17.1%, DSP 22.9%.
limits: Much of the gain is from CoqHammer and backtracking, not only repair rules. Mean time to success 32.89 s vs 3-8 s for others. 59.6% of theorems still fail.
agent_relevance: Big effect size: scaffolding turns a model that nearly always fails into one that solves about 40%. Error types are frequent and mechanical, so code can repair many of them without the model.

source: Lu, Delaware, Zhang (2024) PALM ablations
finding: Each repair rule helps a little; removing backtracking is catastrophic; premise retrieval helps modestly.
numbers: Full PALM 4377 (40.4%). Variants with one repair mechanism disabled: 4249 (39.2%), 4175 (38.5%), 4225 (39.0%), 4094 (37.8%), i.e. 3.0%-6.9% fewer. No backtracking: 702 (6.5%), a 523.5% drop (about 5x). No premise retrieval: 4147 (38.2%), 5.5% fewer. All variants still prove 65.2%-71.5% more than DSP.
limits: One run with GPT-3.5; failure cases: 58% missing premise, 14% premise retrieved but unused, 39% tactics not used (overlapping, from 100 sampled failures).
agent_relevance: Local patching is not enough. The ability to back up and regenerate an earlier step is the main driver. Matches S5 REVISE needing a rollback path, not only a patch.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Lyra: Orchestrating Dual Correction in Automated Theorem Proving
finding: Two correction modes on top of Draft-Sketch-Prove: Tool Correction swaps an LLM-chosen tactic for a prover tool (e.g. Sledgehammer) after failure; Conjecture Correction feeds prover error messages back to rewrite the sketch.
numbers: miniF2F-test 51.2% (valid 55.3%) with human informal proofs, 200 attempts, vs DSP 39.3%; +5.7 over Subgoal-Learning (valid +7.3). GPT-4 informal proofs: 47.9% test, 54.9% valid. Tool Correction adds 4.1 (no CC) and 7.0 (with CC) points with GPT-4 informal proofs; 3.3 and 8.2 points with human informal proofs on test. Without TC and CC, Lyra reduces to DSP.
limits: Conjecture Correction needs more attempts to pay off. Authors' own ablation, no outside replication. Human informal proofs beat GPT-4 ones on test.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of fix: replace a failing step with a stronger tool, or rewrite the plan from the error. Tool swap is cheap and code-driven (fits G2). Plan rewrite helps only with budget.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (DSP), ICLR
finding: The LLM drafts an informal proof, turns it into a formal sketch with open gaps, and an automated prover fills each gap. This is a machine version of a proof plan with holes (a Bundy-style plan).
numbers: miniF2F-test: automated prover alone 20.9%; with sketches from Minerva informal proofs 38.9%; with human informal proofs 39.3% (100 attempts). Sledgehammer-only baseline 9.9% on test.
limits: No repair step: one bad gap fails the whole sketch. Informal proof can be wrong and still help if the structure is right.
agent_relevance: Plan-with-holes then fill is the base pattern. Our S5 can reuse it: keep the plan, repair only the failing hole (see APOLLO, Cobblestone).

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5: truncate-and-resume and RMaxTS
finding: On a Lean error, the generated proof is cut at the first error and the model resumes from the last good tactic. This is built into Monte-Carlo tree search (RMaxTS) with an intrinsic reward for new states.
numbers: miniF2F-test whole-proof pass rate 60.2% (V1: 50.0%, +10.2 points); 51.6% at 128 samples; with RMaxTS 62.7% (abstract states 63.5%). ProofNet test 23.7% single pass (25.3% with RMaxTS), valid 21.6% (25.4%).
limits: Numbers differ across the paper text (62.7% vs 63.5%) depending on setting. ProofAug reports RMaxTS gives under 0.2% over naive retrying at 3200 samples.
agent_relevance: Cut at the first error and keep the good prefix. This is the cheapest repair and keeps the work already verified.

source: Liu (2025) ProofAug: Efficient neural theorem proving via fine-grained proof structure analysis
finding: Parses a full LLM proof into semi-proofs at several granularities. When an automated prover fails at a step, it falls back to a coarser block and retries. An Efficient Recursive Proving (ERP) module adds error-aware retries.
numbers: Isabelle miniF2F-test: 52.5% with at most 100 model queries; gains over DSP baseline of 7.8, 4.1, 3.3 points at budgets 1, 10, 100 (36.5% vs 28.7% at 1). ERP lifts 0-shot ProofAug from 54.5% to 56.1% at 500 queries. Mixed strategies 61.9% in 1700 queries; 66.0% on a curated test set in 2100 requests. Claims RMaxTS shows under 0.2% advantage over naive retrying at 3200 samples. Lifts Kimina-Prover-Preview-Distill-1.5B from 44.3% to 50.4%.
limits: Author-reported, a single preprint. Curated test set changes the benchmark. Gains shrink as budget rises.
agent_relevance: Graduated fallback: fix the finest part, then widen to a coarser block. A concrete shape for S5 escalation.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) APOLLO: Automated LLM and Lean Collaboration for Advanced Formal Reasoning
finding: Agent pipeline: Lean finds errors, fix syntax, isolate failing sub-lemmas, try automated solvers, call the LLM on each remaining goal with a small top-K, reassemble and re-verify, repeat up to a recursion limit.
numbers: Goedel-Prover-SFT: 64.7% at 25,600 samples vs 65.6% with APOLLO at about 362 samples (recursion r=6, 179K samples-total shown in table). Kimina-Prover-Preview-Distill-7B: 70.8% at 1024 samples (4.5M) vs 75.0% with r=6 (1.3M) i.e. +4.2 points. At K=32: 57.6% base; 60.7% r=2; 63.5% r=4; 65.6% r=6. Goedel-V2-8B +0.9 points at similar budget. Claims 84.9% on miniF2F among sub-8B models with budget under 100; o3-mini and o4-mini go from 3-7% to over 40%.
limits: Gains per extra recursion level shrink. Table cells mix budgets; compare only within rows. Gain smaller on the strongest prover (+0.9).
agent_relevance: Best match to our S5: locate the failing part with the checker, fix only that part with a small budget. Repair is far cheaper than resampling.

source: Kasibatla et al. (2026) Cobblestone: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach for Automating Formal Verification, ICSE 26
finding: Uses a failed LLM proof to split the problem: the verified subproofs are kept, unverified ones are replaced by admit, and the LLM is re-prompted only for the remaining pieces. Fail-safe mode uses bullets to find subproofs (43% of proofs in the chain-of-thought runs contain subproofs).
numbers: CoqGym100: 48% vs ChainOfThought 25% (20 samples) and CoqHammer 30%; Wigderson100: 38% vs 19% chain-of-thought and 27% CoqHammer. Cobblestone beats a LinearRegen baseline (regenerate from the first failure) on all datasets, up to +104.8%. Token use: 59.3K vs 99.3K on CoqGym100; 42.0K vs 72.3K on Wigderson100. Cost about $1 per run, 15 min. Beats PALM 15x by 8%, 9% and 2% on three datasets.
limits: Four Coq datasets with leakage controls, 100 theorems each. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 only.
agent_relevance: Keep verified pieces, retry only the failing piece. This beats naive restart-at-first-failure in both accuracy and tokens, a clean ablation for S5.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2: Scaling Formal Theorem Proving with Scaffolded Data Synthesis and Self-Correction
finding: Model is trained to revise its own Lean proof given compiler feedback. Two extra correction rounds are allowed at inference.
numbers: 32B: miniF2F 88.1% pass@32, 90.4% with 2 rounds of self-correction (about +2 points for both model sizes). PutnamBench 43 solved at pass@32, 57 with self-correction (+14). Token cap 30,000 first pass, 40,000 total with correction.
limits: Correction was trained in via RL/data, not prompted. Compute is not equalised with sampling at the same total tokens in the text read.
agent_relevance: Compiler feedback plus revision gives a stable but small gain on easy sets and a larger one on hard sets (PutnamBench).

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
finding: Lemma-style whole proofs refined against Lean feedback, proved lemmas, and self-summaries of past attempts. Three inference levels: light (8-16 refinements), medium, heavy.
numbers: Light setting: each attempt refined 8-16 times, equal to Pass@64x256 budget, 1-2 hours. IMO 2022 P2 (MOHS 151) solved with refinement; without it needs Pass@8192. 78.1% of formalised past IMO problems, miniF2F saturated, over 50% PutnamBench (331/657 in another table), 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems.
limits: Proprietary; compute budget at heavy setting very large and not fully stated. No clean ablation isolating the repair loop beyond the single IMO 2022 example.
agent_relevance: Self-summary of earlier failed attempts carried into the next try is a memory device we could copy for S5 context.

source: Varambally et al. (2026) Hilbert: Recursively Building Formal Proofs with Informal Reasoning, ICLR 2026
finding: An informal reasoner LLM plans and splits a hard problem into subgoals; a Lean prover solves them; verifier feedback drives refinement; a retriever supplies theorems.
numbers: miniF2F 99.2% (+6.6 over best public); PutnamBench 462/660 (70.0%) vs Seed-Prover 50.4%, Goedel-Prover-V2-32B with self-correction 86/644 (13.4%), gpt-oss-120b informal reasoner 88/660 (13.3%). Goedel-V2-32B pass@4 baseline 74.6% -> 90.8% with Hilbert (+16.2); gains over base prover 16.2 to 37.1 points. Gemini 2.5 Pro beats Flash by 3-4 points: the planner matters more than the prover.
limits: Needs a strong informal model; compute heavy; Table 3 compares retrieval on/off for cost only. Not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Plan quality (the informal reasoner) dominated the result. Support for a strong planner with a cheap checker-bound filler.

source: Achim et al. (Harmonic) (2025) Aristotle: IMO-level automated theorem proving
finding: Three parts: Lean proof search (MCTS over states, replaces sorry), lemma-based informal reasoning that formalises lemmas and iterates on formal feedback, and a geometry solver.
numbers: Gold-medal-equivalent on IMO 2025: formal solutions to 5 of 6 problems reported.
limits: Proprietary system; no ablation of the iteration loop in the text read.
agent_relevance: Another confirmation that decompose-into-lemmas then iterate on checker feedback is the current winning loop.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to review and correct its answer makes results worse. Gains in earlier papers came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: standard 75.9; oracle self-correct 84.3; intrinsic 3 calls 75.1, 5 calls 74.7. CommonSenseQA: 75.8 standard, 38.1 after round 1 intrinsic. GPT-4 GSM8K: 95.5 standard, 91.5 and 89.0 intrinsic; with oracle 97.5. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 -> 88.0 -> 90.0. GSM8K GPT-3.5 keeps first answer 74.7% of time; when it changes, correct->incorrect is more common than the reverse.
limits: Reasoning QA, not formal proof. Oracle numbers shown only to explain why earlier papers looked good.
agent_relevance: Core support for G2 and G3. In proof repair the Lean error is the non-model signal. Without that, revision hurts.

source: Ringer, Palmskog, Sergey, Gligoric, Tatlock (2019/2020) QED at Large: A Survey of Engineering of Formally Verified Software
finding: Survey of proof engineering. Describes proof planning (Bundy 1988) as a way to use plans to guide proofs with similar structure, with critics (Ireland 1996) that reuse information from failing proofs. Says critics can be seen as proof repair. Describes proof repair as program repair for proofs; PUMPKIN PATCH generalises example patches.
numbers: No experiments. Key point: in proof repair the specification (the theorem) is always available, which removes the overfitting problem of program repair.
limits: Survey; a mix of claims not tested. Proof planning is described briefly.
agent_relevance: Gives the lineage: planning with critics (Bundy, Ireland) to symbolic repair (PUMPKIN PATCH, Ringer) to LLM repair (Baldur, PALM). A critic is a rule triggered by a plan failure; our checker plus rule table is the same shape.

source: Ringer, Palmskog et al. (2020) QED at Large: tools for proof reuse and evolution (IsaPlanner, rippling)
finding: IsaPlanner is a proof planner for Isabelle with support for rippling, a technique for automatic induction. Proof planning was designed for automated provers and reached interactive provers.
numbers: None given.
limits: Description only. No benchmark numbers on planning success in the survey text.
agent_relevance: Older machine systems used explicit plans with failure-triggered critics. No modern study found that re-tests rippling or critics inside an LLM loop.

source: Bundy (1988) The Use of Explicit Plans to Guide Inductive Proofs, CADE 9
finding: Founding paper of proof planning: a proof method has preconditions and effects, and a planner assembles methods into a proof plan; when a method fails, critics suggest a patch. Cited and described by the 2020 survey; not opened itself.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; description via c17.
agent_relevance: The idea of plan, execute, patch with a named critic for each failure type.

source: Ireland and Bundy (1996) Productive use of failure in inductive proof
finding: Proof critics: when a planned method fails, the pattern of failure suggests a fix (for example a lemma, a generalisation, or a case split). Known only through the Ringer survey citation; not opened.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A table mapping failure type to fix is the same design as PALM's error taxonomy (c04) and could be our S5 rule table.

source: Kasibatla et al. (2026) Cobblestone, comparison to other LLM tools
finding: The paper compares to PALM and Rango under the same data-leakage controls, and notes Cobblestone proves theorems the other tools cannot.
numbers: Non-LLM tools together prove 33% (CoqGym100) so added value of Cobblestone over all non-LLM is 54.5%; 25.0%, 40.0%, 14.6% on the other three. Proverbot9001 and CoqHammer 19.8% and 26.6% on full CoqGym.
limits: Authors of Cobblestone include Baldur and Rango authors (shared lab). PALM was run 15 times to match budget.
agent_relevance: Tools overlap only partly, so a portfolio of different repair routes proves more than one route.

source: Kasibatla et al. (2026) Cobblestone, retrieval and custom repair prompts
finding: The paper reports that adding external information (retrieval, custom repair prompts, backtracking) increases its success rate.
numbers: Cobblestone proves up to 58% (CoqGym subset) and 55% (coq-wigderson) when given a proof structure and relevant lemmas.
limits: That figure uses extra information (structure and lemmas); not the headline 48%/38%.
agent_relevance: Repair gains depend on what extra context the model is shown. Cite which context before comparing runs.

source: Thakur et al. (2025) Rango: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Proving for Automated Software Verification, ICSE 25
finding: Step-wise Coq proving where each step retrieves earlier proofs and lemmas from the same project (BM25 and TF-IDF). Not a repair method, but the retrieval of similar proofs is a form of reuse.
numbers: Proves 32.0% of theorems on its benchmark, 29% more than Tactician, 66% more than Proverbot9001, 4% more than another LLM tool. Adding relevant proofs to the context gives a 47% increase in theorems proven.
limits: Abstract-level numbers read from first pages; the full table was not examined. Premise retrieval, not error repair.
agent_relevance: Reusing earlier proofs as context is a large effect (+47%) and adjacent to repair-by-analogy (PUMPKIN PATCH idea).

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Lyra, effect of informal proof quality
finding: Quality of the plan (informal proof) changes the final result: human informal proofs beat GPT-4 ones on test.
numbers: Test 51.2% (human informal) vs 47.9% (GPT-4 informal) at 200 attempts; valid 55.3% vs 54.9%. With Codex vs GPT-4 formaliser, GPT-4 adds 5.3 (valid) and 0.4 (test) points.
limits: Small differences on test; one dataset.
agent_relevance: Support for treating the plan as a checked object: the plan itself is a place where errors enter.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) DSP, compare to others cited in the text of Lyra and ProofAug
finding: Reference table in ProofAug of Isabelle methods on miniF2F-test with sample budgets.
numbers: DSP 39.3% (100 samples, Codex); Subgoal-XL 39.3% at 64 and 56.1% at 16384 samples; LEGO-Prover 50.0% (100); Lyra 47.1% at 100 and 51.2% at 200; ProofAug 52.5% at 100. DSP baseline with deepseek-math-7b-base 28.7% at 1 and 40.6% at 10; ProofAug 0-shot 36.5% at 1 and 44.7% at 10.
limits: Different base models and budgets across rows; compare with care.
agent_relevance: Shows how much of the progress comes from structure-aware repair at fixed budgets, not only bigger models.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5, sampling vs tree search
finding: Tree search with truncate-and-resume gives a small gain over plain whole-proof sampling at the same model.
numbers: miniF2F-test: single-pass RL model 60.2% vs RMaxTS 62.7% (+2.5). ProofNet test 23.7% vs 25.3% (+1.6 in the numbers given in the paper). ProofAug later argues the gap over naive retrying is under 0.2% at 3200 samples.
limits: Competing claims about whether the search adds value. Different budget definitions.
agent_relevance: Do not assume elaborate search beats resampling. Measure it against a plain retry baseline.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, why accuracy drops
finding: The model cannot judge its own reasoning, and the review prompt biases it to switch answers.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 -> 38.1 after round 1, 41.8 after round 2 with the intrinsic prompt. GPT-4: stays on the initial answer more often.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Benchmarks where oracle-based work was previously reported; prompts follow the source papers.
agent_relevance: Explains why G2 requires code to say whether a failure happened. In theorem proving the compiler plays the oracle role legitimately.

source: Not yet searched: LLM-based proof repair across proof-assistant version changes (Ringer REPLica/PUMPKIN lineage, Proofster, type-equivalence repair)
finding: No source opened this session for symbolic proof repair tools (PUMPKIN PATCH, Pumpkin Pi, REPLica) beyond their description in the survey, and no study found that tests LLMs on proof repair after library or spec change. The WebSearch budget was used up before this gap could be checked.
numbers: None.
limits: Gap noted so a later pass can fill it.
agent_relevance: Open question for the file: does LLM repair work when the spec changes, not only when a fresh attempt fails?
